items.title: Morning Briefing: Nov. 17, 2026
items.excerpt: Here's a rundown of all the news you need to start your Tuesday, including Germany's call on Israel to allow more aid to reach Gaza before winter, US President Donald Trump's indication of a possible meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his Asia trip, and Jordan's blocking of the Telegram messaging application as part of efforts to prevent the spread of “extremism and radicalization." German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul called on Israel to allow significantly more humanitarian aid to reach the Gaza Strip to prevent further deterioration as rainy and stormy winter months approach. Speaking to reporters ahead of an EU foreign ministers’ meeting in Brussels, Wadephul said the latest developments in the Middle East, especially the humanitarian crisis in Gaza, will be discussed by the ministers. "We are all concerned about the situation with the coming rainy and stormy winter months," he said. "The European message is clear: it is urgently necessary that significantly more humanitarian aid arrives in the Gaza Strip so that the humanitarian situation does not deteriorate further." Wadephul noted that he had raised the issue with colleagues last week at the G7 foreign ministers meeting and remains in constant contact with Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar. - Trump says he 'may' meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during Asia trip US President Donald Trump said he "may" meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China during an upcoming diplomatic tour of Asia. "We could ... have a chance to accomplish a lot," Trump told reporters about his meetings with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin as he departed the White House, adding that a possible meeting with the North Korean leader depends on Kim and Xi. The US president said his itinerary will be focused largely on economic issues. Trump will arrive in the Philippine capital Manila on Tuesday for talks with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), a regional bloc, and the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad), a diplomatic partnership made up of the US, Australia, India and Japan.

The trip follows Republican losses in the US midterm elections and comes amid scrutiny of the administration’s handling of Nvidia. Trump is due in Manila on Tuesday for his first meeting with the Quad leaders of Japan, Australia and India. The group has not met at leader level for two years. Its discussions could cover maritime security, export restrictions, critical minerals and artificial intelligence, ahead of Trump’s participation in a US-ASEAN summit. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned against any redistribution of global influence, while China has described the meeting as significant for international stability. ###### Sources: Associated Press, Reuters Japan scrambled fighter jets and protested to Moscow after two suspected Russian military aircraft entered Japanese airspace near Okinoshima island off Fukuoka early Tuesday. The Defense Ministry said the planes entered separately for several minutes, prompting warnings from Japanese fighters before continuing through the Tsushima Strait towards the western Pacific. South Korea also deployed fighters after several Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone over the Sea of Japan. Seoul said the aircraft did not violate South Korean territorial airspace, distinguishing its response from Japan’s reported incursion. Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara called the apparent violation of Japanese sovereignty unacceptable and said Tokyo had lodged a strong diplomatic protest. The incidents occurred ahead of a planned meeting between the leaders of Russia, China and the United States at the APEC forum in Shenzhen. Crimea’s Moscow-appointed governor, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed the attack, while Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said minor damage was being assessed. Reports differed over the extent of damage, and roughly 2,000 vehicles were reportedly stranded. Kyiv meanwhile faced repeated Russian air raids, with at least seven people killed and power cut to 50,000 residents. The escalation followed renewed diplomatic talks that have made little progress. Moscow continues to demand Ukrainian territorial concessions, while Kyiv has rejected surrendering territory. ###### Sources: BBC, The Guardian US Vice President JD Vance has insisted the conflict with Iran will not become a prolonged war, even as a third American aircraft carrier arrives in the Middle East. The USS Theodore Roosevelt joins two other carriers while diplomatic efforts to end hostilities and reopen the Strait of Hormuz remain stalled. ... The deployment underscores the gap between Washington’s assurances of an eventual exit and its continuing military build-up. US intelligence indicates Iran is considering plans to attack senior Trump administration officials in Washington using a radioactive dirty bomb or chemical weapon, according to seven American officials. The intelligence reportedly identifies potential targets and locations but officials say there is no evidence Tehran has decided to proceed or has the personnel to carry out an attack. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said there were currently no credible threats to the US homeland. Iran’s UN mission rejected allegations concerning chemical weapons but did not directly address the reported dirty bomb planning. US authorities have nevertheless held contingency meetings, while intelligence suggesting bomb-making materials may already be inside the country remains disputed. The warnings emerge amid stalled negotiations to end the US-Iran war and lift Washington’s blockade of Iranian ports. Officials are also assessing separate intelligence concerning possible chemical attacks on American troops in the Middle East, raising concerns about the conflict extending beyond its current theatres. Iran-backed Houthi rebels have gained control of Yemen’s Bab al-Mandab Strait after Saudi-backed government forces withdrew from the Red Sea coast to defend Aden. The strategic waterway normally carries around 12% of global trade and the advance threatens to further disrupt shipping already affected by the US-Iran war.

items.title: US Fed Chair Warsh's true test begins now - The Economic Times
items.excerpt: Last Updated: Nov 17, 2026, 10:36:00 AM IST Orlando, Florida: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh is facing the biggest test of his tenure so far. Just as the economic case for accelerating interest rate hikes is strengthening, political pressure to go easier has returned. Warsh officially replaced Jerome Powell as Fed chair on May 22. Most economic signs since then have indicated that tighter monetary policy is needed. Inflation has remained sticky and above target, largely due to persistently high energy prices caused by the Iran war. The AI investment boom has fueled record corporate earnings and stock prices, while the labor market and wider economy appear to be in good shape. The unemployment rate in October was just 4.1%, and annualized GDP growth in the third quarter accelerated to 3.4%. But the Fed has raised rates only once under Warsh's watch, a 25-basis-point increase in September. ... The timing puts Warsh in a difficult position. As several Fed officials have pointed out over the last two weeks, there is still a lot of "work to do" to get inflation down, as the October consumer price index print testified. Inflation was above forecasts for a third month, as high energy prices passed through the economy into "core" goods and services. So much so that a rare 50-bps hike next month is now on the table, and an additional 45 bps of tightening by the end of next year has been added to the rate futures curve. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield is back above 5%, and the 2-year yield's leap of 35 basis points last week was one of the biggest in decades.

items.title: Chicago Fed President: Persistent High Inflation Could Be ‘Painful to Try to Get Rid Of’
items.excerpt: Andrew Montequin | November 16, 2026, 6:14 pm Inflation has been above the Federal Reserve Bank’s target since February 2021. Those five and a half years have seen periods of progress and setbacks. But the direction inflation is headed now — with high prices expanding beyond temporary shocks from tariffs and the Iran war — is raising eyebrows. “At this moment, we’ve got to be very cognizant that we’re dancing on the edge of something that’s hard and potentially painful to get rid of,” said Austan Goolsbee, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago. ... The consumer price index for all items rose 0.4% in one month, according to data released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) last week. Last year’s government shutdown prevented the BLS from comparing prices to October 2025. But estimates place the annual inflation rate near 4%, double the Fed’s target. When higher-than-desired inflation sticks around that long, “it’s even more painful to try to get rid of,” Goolsbee said. “If people start taking for granted that inflation is going to be this high next year, the year after, et cetera, then they start factoring it into their decisions.” If the expectation of sustained inflation hangs over businesses’ decisions on topics like wage negotiations and cost planning, the central bank can have a harder time bringing inflation down. That doesn’t mean there hasn’t been progress in the past half decade. “There have been times when we were making progress, and I thought we were on the path back to 2%,” Goolsbee said. Goolsbee pointed to “negative shocks,” including tariffs and high prices of oil, that knocked prices off of this path. But he sees a different trend emerging now, where services not directly connected to these shocks are starting to see inflation. Goolsbee gave health insurance as an example of a service that’s seeing price spikes. “Health insurance inflation is not coming from tariffs, is not coming from oil prices, is not coming from any of the things that you could envision turning on a dime,” Goolsbee said. “Historically, things like health insurance, when they get ramped up they stay up and they keep rising.” As for fighting inflation, the “pain” Goolsbee referenced could manifest in the form of a recession. Other than supply-chain disruptions and subsequent “healing” during recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic, “the only times we’ve ever gotten inflation down significantly have come with nasty recessions. The slowing of the economy is the thing that slowed the inflation,” Goolsbee said. Now, all eyes are on the Federal Open Market Committee to see just how high — if at all — they are willing to raise interest rates to tame inflation. “Demand overheating, which might be more in the style of AI data center buildout driving up the price of construction, computer chips, electronic equipment, … raising interest rates slows the economy and does help cure that type of inflation,” Goolsbee said.

items.title: Hammack Favors Gradual Fed Hikes, Cites Firms’ Growing Willingness to Raise Prices | EconoTimes
items.excerpt: By Miriam Hart Nov 17, 2026, 1:49 AM UTC ... Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented from the Fed’s Oct. 28 decision to hold rates, favoring a quarter-point increase as she raised concerns about firms passing price rises to customers. In a Nov. 16 interview with Bloomberg Television, Hammack said businesses appeared increasingly inclined to shift higher prices to customers. She reiterated her preference for a gradual pace of interest-rate moves. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) kept its target range at 3.75% to 4.00%. The vote was 10-2; Fed Governor Lisa D. Cook also dissented, with both her and Hammack favoring a 0.25-percentage-point increase. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported that the seasonally adjusted Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose 0.4% in October from the previous month, following a 0.6% increase in September. The index excluding food and energy advanced 0.3% in October, matching its monthly gains in August and September. The October release lacks the usual year-over-year changes for affected series because the BLS did not collect October 2025 data during a lapse in appropriations. The CPI is separate from the personal consumption expenditures price index, whose annual change the Fed uses to assess its longer-run 2% inflation goal.

items.title: Grocery inflation is set go up as input costs rise
items.excerpt: Conditions are ripe for grocery inflation to rise at a relatively fast clip over the coming months as persistently high energy costs and rough climate conditions pose challenges for food producers and retailers, Ricky Volpe, professor of agribusiness at California Polytechnic State University, said Thursday during a briefing hosted by FMI — The Food Industry Association. The high price of diesel and the start of an El Niño weather pattern that meteorologists expect to be especially powerful are likely to disrupt supply chains, putting upward pressure on food prices and pushing up food-at-home prices at a faster-than-average pace at least into early 2027, Volpe said. "There's not a whole lot that's moving in the right direction in terms of keeping food prices flat or down right now … it would surprise me to see food prices go flat or trend down in the next four or five months," he said. The Producer Price Index, which tracks wholesale prices and provides clues about the future direction of retail prices, has been rising in recent months, with costs for transportation, commodities, energy and storage all going up, Volpe noted. ... Grocery inflation has bumped around on a month-to-month basis in 2026 but rose last month at the fastest pace since April, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported last week. Volpe noted that the 0.4% jump in grocery inflation recorded in October was "pretty substantial," adding that if the metric increased at that rate every month for a year, it would translate into a 5-percentage-point boost on an annual basis. The BLS did not report year-over-year figures for inflation last month because it did not capture data for the same period in 2025 due to the federal government shutdown.

items.title: Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid Says Inflation Remains Too High | EconoTimes
items.excerpt: U.S. inflation remained above the Federal Reserve’s 2% objective, and Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City President Jeff Schmid said Sunday that reducing price growth had become more difficult since August. He made the remarks at the National Credit Union Management Association 2026 Conference in Kohala Coast, Hawai’i. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index rose 3.6% from a year earlier in September, the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) reported. The index excluding food and energy increased 3.1% over the same period. For the month, the overall index rose 0.5% and the core measure gained 0.3%. Schmid cited a 5.7% annualized rise in consumer price index (CPI) prices over the three months through October. That is a three-month pace, not a year-over-year rate. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said October CPI rose 0.4% from the previous month, seasonally adjusted. It did not publish a 12-month rate because October 2025 comparison data were unavailable after a lapse in federal appropriations. Schmid described the labor market as largely balanced, with wage growth around 3% and about one available job for each job seeker. He pointed to higher oil costs, tariffs, demand tied to artificial intelligence infrastructure and rising health care expenses as sources of price pressure. Employer health-benefit costs, he said, had risen more than 6% over the past year, their fastest pace in more than 20 years. For durable goods, Schmid said prices advanced 2.9% in September; only the pandemic-era ... Schmid said supply disruptions can have a greater effect on prices when demand is strong, while the Fed can influence demand. “Demand always plays a role in inflation,” he said. His prepared remarks did not recommend a specific interest-rate move.

He's seeking a break from a series of setbacks at home, including a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry and a scandal that has shaken the global artificial intelligence industry. Trump’s arrival in Manila on Tuesday evening is his first stop on a three-day trip that will also take him to China. That's where he'll hold first-ever trilateral talks with the presidents of China and Russia. Trump told reporters on Monday that he might meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un this week, too. ... First new DC delegate since 1991 hopes that Democratic victories mean statehood is coming WASHINGTON (AP) — The last time the District of Columbia had a freshman delegate going through new member orientation on Capitol Hill, the Soviet Union still existed, George H.W. Bush was president and the first Gulf War in Iraq hadn’t started yet. Now Robert White Jr. is stepping into the role held by Eleanor Holmes Norton, a legendary advocate for Washington, D.C., who is retiring after 36 years. White was only eight when she started the job. Speaking to The Associated Press in between orientation events, White said his priorities are the same — statehood for the city and improving the district’s economic situation. But he arrives at a time when Democrats have an unexpectedly overwhelming advantage in both chambers, tilting the political landscape in D.C.’s favor. ... Trump's pick for Navy secretary likely to face Iran war questions during confirmation hearing WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump’s pick to lead the U.S. Navy is scheduled to testify before the Senate Armed Services Committee. Tuesday's hearing will be the first step in a nomination process that could turn into a fierce debate over the Iran war and military transparency. Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao is a Trump loyalist and combat veteran. He's seeking the permanent top civilian job while Republicans still control Congress following their resounding defeat in the midterm elections. Cao will need a waiver from Congress to serve as Navy secretary because he left active-duty service less than seven years ago. ... Trump administration moves to block China from indirect access to American AI technology WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration has issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers. The move aims to limit China's use of U.S. chips for training AI models. The rule was announced Monday. It follows Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang's resignation over links to a Chinese executive suspected of funneling U.S. chips to Chinese AI companies. The Bureau of Industry and Security states the rule ensures existing restrictions aren't bypassed through remote computing in third countries. Overseas data centers serving countries like China and Russia must now perform due diligence, with new licensing requirements for certain countries.

items.excerpt: Published: 12:00 AM EST November 17, 2026 ... The nationwide grounding of flights last week will only intensify scrutiny of the Federal Aviation Administration, which has been under a spotlight since a midair collision last year that killed dozens. The agency has been plagued for decades by underfunding, outdated technology and staffing shortages. Yet isolated technical problems went largely unnoticed by the flying public, even as experts saw them as signs of serious trouble brewing. The FAA says it is trying to make long-overdue upgrades by the end of President Donald Trump's second term with $12.5 billion Congress approved last year. But experts warn that rushing the process could make things worse. “What we’re seeing has been decades in the making,” said Mike McCormick, who used to oversee air traffic control at the agency before becoming a professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University. Improving aviation safety has been a focus of the Trump administration since last year’s midair collision outside the nation's capital killed 67 people. A prolonged government shutdown last year highlighted the chronic shortage of controllers, while communications disruptions that affected Newark Liberty International Airport last spring, and again in September, also raised concerns.

November 17, 2026 ### Justice Department Finalizes Immigration Appeals Overhaul, Says There Is No Constitutional Right to a Board Appeal The Justice Department's Executive Office for Immigration Review released a final rule on Monday, Nov. 16, overhauling the Board of Immigration Appeals — most appeals will now be summarily dismissed without an opinion unless the Board votes to take them, the filing deadline drops from 30 days to 10, and the rule states plainly that there is no constitutional due process right to an administrative appeal before the Board. November 17, 2026 ### Senate Votes 70-27 to Advance Bipartisan Permitting Overhaul, Clearing Key Hurdle Toward Final Passage The Senate voted 70-27 on Monday evening, Nov. 16, to invoke cloture on the Capito substitute amendment to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, ending debate on the negotiated text of the nearly 500-page permitting overhaul and moving it closer to a final passage vote in the lame-duck session. November 17, 2026 ### Senate Confirms Daniel Domenico to the 10th Circuit, 51-46, as Republicans Race to Fill Appeals Seats Before Democrats Take Over The Republican-led Senate voted 51-46 on Monday evening, Nov. 16, to confirm U.S. District Judge Daniel Domenico of Colorado to the Denver-based 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals — the latest step in a lame-duck push to fill appeals-court vacancies before Democrats take control of the chamber in January. November 17, 2026 ### Federal Judge Throws Out Trump's Visa Rules for Foreign Students and Journalists, Vacates Rule in Full A federal judge in Boston on Monday, Nov. 16, vacated in full the Trump administration's rule that would have capped foreign students and exchange visitors at four years in the United States and foreign journalists at 240 days, ruling that the Department of Homeland Security acted arbitrarily and beyond its authority. November 17, 2026 ### White House Orders Agencies to Get Its Sign-Off Before Any Employee Testifies to Congress White House Counsel Will Scharf issued a one-page memo on Monday, Nov. 16, directing every executive department and agency to obtain approval from the White House Counsel's office and the Office of Legislative Affairs before any employee agrees to appear before a congressional committee — seven weeks before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress.

items.excerpt: Grammy nominations snub Harry Styles and hip-hop, while surprises include Dolly Parton NEW YORK (AP) — The 2027 Grammy Award nominees have been announced, sparking inevitable discussions about snubs and surprises. Notably, there's no hip-hop in most general field categories, a shift from last year. Women dominate many major categories, with only Bruno Mars breaking the trend. Harry Styles did not receive a nomination and Noah Kahan only received one. Beyoncé makes history with her 100th career nomination. Dolly Parton and Tim Curry receive posthumous nominations. A new category for Asian pop music performance has been introduced, but BTS chose not to participate and thus wasn't nominated. The awards will air on Feb. 7. Glenn Close marvels at honorary Oscar as Ridley Scott and indie producers also get statuettes LOS ANGELES (AP) — Glenn Close has finally received her first Oscar, an honorary award at the Governors Awards in Los Angeles. Close, 79, was honored alongside director Ridley Scott, animator Floyd Norman, and producers Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler. Close, who has been nominated eight times without a win, expressed deep gratitude for the recognition. John Malkovich, her “Dangerous Liaisons” co-star, presented the award, praising her remarkable career. Matt Damon honored Ridley Scott, who accepted via video. The event, which often kicks off Hollywood’s awards season, also celebrated Vachon and Koffler's contributions to independent cinema and Norman's groundbreaking work in animation. Robert Pattinson is named the seventh James Bond, taking over from Daniel Craig Robert Pattinson has been unveiled as the next James Bond, becoming the seventh actor to play the iconic British spy and the first since Amazon MGM took over the beloved film franchise. The naming of Pattinson on Monday comes during the longest hiatus in 007 history and ends years of rampant speculation about who would inherit the role from Daniel Craig. Pattinson described getting to play Bond as “the honour of a lifetime.” Denis Villeneuve, who will direct the next film, praised Pattinson as having “a timeless soul.” ... Raye leads 2027 Grammy nominations, followed by Rosalía, Ella Langley, Olivia Rodrigo and more NEW YORK (AP) — The Recording Academy announced the 2027 Grammy Award nominations on Monday, with English singer-songwriter Raye leading the pack. She's up for 11 awards, including record, song and album of the year. This ties Beyoncé’s record for the most nominations in a single year by a woman artist. Raye’s album “This Music May Contain Hope” has earned her critical acclaim. Spanish singer Rosalía follows with nine nominations, while Ella Langley, Miranda Lambert, Olivia Rodrigo and Phoebe Bridgers each have seven. Bruno Mars, Leon Thomas and 2026’s best new artist winner Olivia Dean have six nominations each. The 2027 Grammy Awards will air Feb. 7 on ABC, Disney+, and Hulu. ... PARIS (AP) — French actor Gérard Depardieu says he is dropping his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set. He will accept the 18-month suspended sentence and has issued an apology. Depardieu was convicted in May 2025 for groping a set decorator and an assistant during the filming of “Les Volets Verts” in 2021. The court ordered him to pay fines and list his name in the national sex offender database.
